name: Dosage
seoDesc: Dosage: work out frequency from your weight and the dose. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: frequency is what the Dosage calculator works out, and it gets there from your weight, the dose and the total daily dose. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Dosage calculator work?
sections.html:
The Dosage calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports frequency in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in your weight, the dose and the total daily dose.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Dosage calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Frequency=dosage × your weight ÷ dose
Liquid dose=dosage × your weight ÷ (frequency × medicine concentration)
Liquid dose=dose ÷ medicine concentration
Dosage=total daily dose ÷ your weight
Total liquid dose=total daily dose ÷ medicine concentration

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Your weight = 10 kg, Dosage = 10 mg, Frequency set to Once per day and Dose = 10 mg. The calculator returns Total daily dose = 100 mg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Total daily dose = 100 mg should be roughly the size you expected from Your weight = 10 kg and Dosage = 10 mg.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • Shown in milliliters, and convertible to any of the 40 units on that chip.
  • Shown in milligrams per milliliter, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • Shown in milligrams, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Shown in milliliters, and convertible to any of the 40 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in milligrams
  • Mass, opening in milligrams
  • Mass, opening in milligrams
  • Density, opening in milligrams per milliliter
  • Volume, opening in milliliters
  • Volume, opening in milliliters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Dosage calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — your weight, the dose and the total daily dose — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Dosage calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns frequency, derived from your weight, the dose and the total daily dose. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Dosage calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for your weight, the dose and the total daily dose, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your weight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your weight opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total daily dose = 100 mg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Dosage calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
